body:
Three Movements with Different Immediate Objectives

Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda shared Gandhi's method of nonviolent resistance, but they did not arise from the same grievance or involve the same opposing parties.

Understanding their differences is essential because the events occurred close together and are often discussed as a single phase of the national movement.

Comparative Study

FeatureChamparanAhmedabadKheda
Year191719181918
LocationBiharGujaratGujarat
Main participantsIndigo tenant cultivatorsCotton textile workersPeasant cultivators
Opposing partyEuropean indigo plantersIndian mill ownersColonial revenue authorities
Main grievanceCompulsory indigo cultivationWage disputeRevenue demands after crop failure
Form of resistanceInquiry and peaceful defianceStrike and fastCollective revenue non-payment
Major resultAbolition of tinkathia35% wage increase through arbitrationConditional revenue suspension for poorer cultivators

Important Persons and Their Correct Associations

  • Rajkumar Shukla: Peasant who persuaded Gandhi to visit Champaran.
  • Rajendra Prasad and Brajkishore Prasad: Important associates in the Champaran inquiry.
  • Anasuya Sarabhai: Organiser and supporter of Ahmedabad textile workers.
  • Ambalal Sarabhai: Prominent industrialist representing the mill owners in Ahmedabad.
  • Vallabhbhai Patel: Principal associate of Gandhi in the Kheda campaign and an organiser of peasants in Gujarat.
  • Gandhi: Leader or principal mediator in all 3 movements.

These associations help distinguish the events. A statement connecting Rajkumar Shukla primarily with the Ahmedabad wage dispute, or Anasuya Sarabhai primarily with the Champaran indigo inquiry, would incorrectly combine people and movements.

Common Features of the Three Campaigns

Despite their different grievances, the movements followed several common principles.

1. Local Problems Became Organised Public Issues

The movements began with grievances experienced by identifiable groups. Indigo tenants faced compulsory cultivation, textile workers faced an unresolved wage dispute, and Kheda cultivators disputed revenue collection following crop failure.

Local leaders and volunteers helped convert these individual difficulties into organised collective demands.

2. Gandhi Emphasised an Understanding of the Facts

Gandhi did not treat every complaint as sufficient justification for immediate confrontation. He investigated the situation, consulted local workers and considered the claims involved.

This was particularly evident in Champaran, where cultivators' statements formed an important part of the official inquiry, and in Ahmedabad, where Gandhi examined the basis of the workers' wage demand.

3. Participants Were Expected to Maintain Nonviolent Discipline

Gandhi's method required resistance without physical attacks on opponents. Participants were asked to remain firm even when their actions involved hardship, loss of income or government punishment.

In Ahmedabad, this meant continuing a peaceful strike. In Kheda, it meant accepting the consequences of withholding land revenue. In Champaran, it involved refusing an official order while accepting legal responsibility.

4. Resistance and Negotiation Were Used Together

None of the movements required the rejection of all discussion with opponents. Gandhi combined organised public pressure with opportunities for settlement.

Champaran resulted in an official inquiry and agrarian reform. Ahmedabad ended through arbitration. Kheda concluded after the authorities agreed to suspend collection for poorer cultivators, although the practical relief was limited.

How the Campaigns Contributed to Mass Politics

The three movements helped establish a more direct relationship between national political leadership and the everyday grievances of ordinary people.

Previously, many political campaigns had been led mainly by educated professionals and urban organisations. The involvement of indigo cultivators, textile workers and peasants demonstrated the possibility of broadening participation beyond these groups.

Each movement also helped develop local political organisation. Lawyers and volunteers worked alongside cultivators in Champaran. Workers in Ahmedabad gained experience in disciplined collective action and arbitration. Peasants and public workers in Kheda strengthened their organisational networks in Gujarat.

The results were not identical or equally complete. Champaran secured a substantial change to the indigo cultivation system. Ahmedabad achieved a wage settlement. Kheda obtained limited revenue relief, but its practical implementation disappointed Gandhi.

Nevertheless, the campaigns demonstrated that specific economic grievances could provide a basis for organised nonviolent political participation.

Relationship with the Wider National Movement

These local interventions preceded the expansion of Gandhian protest into an all-India struggle.

In 1919, Gandhi organised the Rowlatt Satyagraha against repressive legislation. Unlike the earlier movements, it sought to mobilise opposition across different regions of India around a common political issue.

The local campaigns of 1917-1918 therefore helped establish Gandhi's reputation and practical experience before the larger national agitations that followed.

Avoid confusing local and national campaigns. Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda were important early Gandhian interventions, but they should not individually be described as Gandhi's first nationwide satyagraha. That distinction belongs to the Rowlatt Satyagraha of 1919.

Essential Distinctions for Objective Questions

  • Indigo cultivation versus land revenue: Champaran opposed compulsory crop cultivation under European planters; Kheda challenged government revenue collection during agricultural distress.
  • Peasant movement versus labour movement: Champaran and Kheda involved cultivators; Ahmedabad involved industrial workers.
  • Different meanings of percentages: Tinkathia required indigo cultivation on 15% of the holding; Ahmedabad produced a 35% wage award; the Kheda revenue rule involved a crop assessment of 25% or less of normal.
  • Different forms of settlement: Champaran produced agrarian legal reform, Ahmedabad produced an arbitration award, and Kheda resulted in limited suspension of revenue collection for poorer cultivators.
  • Different local leaders: Rajkumar Shukla was central to bringing Gandhi to Champaran; Anasuya Sarabhai organised Ahmedabad workers; Vallabhbhai Patel was a principal organiser in Kheda.

Conclusion

Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda demonstrated that satyagraha could address different forms of injustice without abandoning its central principles of truth, nonviolence, collective organisation and willingness to negotiate.

Champaran established an important precedent in agrarian reform, Ahmedabad demonstrated disciplined industrial action, and Kheda strengthened peasant organisation in Gujarat. Together, they helped prepare the ground for the wider participation of ordinary Indians in the national movement.

Prelims focus

  • Champaran, 1917: Bihar, indigo cultivators, tinkathia system.
  • Ahmedabad, 1918: Gujarat, textile workers, 35% wage settlement.
  • Kheda, 1918: Gujarat, land revenue relief after crop failure.
  • Organisation: Gujarat Sabha was associated with the Kheda movement.
  • National expansion: Rowlatt Satyagraha, 1919.
  • Trap: The 25% crop-assessment criterion in Kheda and the 25% refund of certain unlawful payments in Champaran were entirely different matters.

K. pictures.caption: The common method of investigation, disciplined resistance and negotiation across the early satyagrahas.

title: Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda: Comparison, Outcomes and Lessons for Mass Politics
